verdicts.quote: Line 88: 'new byte[(int)contentLength]' - can be up to 2^31-1 bytes (2GB). No sanity check on declared size vs. actual stream size.
verdicts.why: F02 is about exactly this mechanism: a length field taken from the untrusted stream (contentLength, read via readUnsignedInt) is used directly as the size of the byte[] allocation in readBytes(), and the array is allocated before any check that the declared number of bytes is actually available in the stream. The finding names the attacker action ('An attacker can declare a 2GB array to exhaust memory') and explicitly states there is no check of the declared size against the actual stream size, which is the 'buffer created before the payload has been shown to exist' half of the mechanism.

verdicts.quote: readFieldValue() calls readTable() which calls readFieldValue() recursively with no depth limit.
verdicts.why: F08 is squarely about the mutual-recursion-without-depth-counter mechanism: readFieldValue() -> readTable()/readArray() -> readFieldValue(), driven by nesting in the attacker-supplied frame, with no depth accounting ('No MAX_NESTING_DEPTH or depth counter. Recursive calls at lines 181 and 184 are unbounded'), and the exploitable outcome is StackOverflowError from deeply nested tables/arrays. That is the input-controlled cycle depth described by D2, not a passing mention.
